Stater
STAY-ter
n. (Greek)
Greek statēr, “a standard,” from histēmi (to stand). A Greek silver coin equal to four drachmas or two didrachmas (two temple-tax half-shekels); the coin found by Peter in the fish’s mouth in Matt 17:27.

📖 Biblical Definition

The stater is the Greek silver coin worth four drachmas or two didrachmas—exactly the amount needed to pay the temple tax for two persons. The word appears once in the New Testament, in one of the most singular incidents of Christ’s earthly ministry: the temple-tax episode of Matthew 17:24-27. The narrative: when Christ and the disciples have come to Capernaum, the collectors of the temple half-shekel tax (the didrachma) approach Peter and ask: doth not your master pay tribute? Peter answers, yes. When Peter comes into the house, Christ anticipates him and asks: what thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers? Peter saith unto him, Of strangers. Jesus saith unto him, Then are the children free. The reasoning is christologically deep: Christ is the Son of the King whose temple-tax is being collected; the Son of God owes no temple-tax to His own Father’s house. But Christ chooses not to claim the exemption: notwithstanding, lest we should offend them, go thou to the sea, and cast an hook, and take up the fish that first cometh up; and when thou hast opened his mouth, thou shalt find a piece of money (a stater): that take, and give unto them for me and thee. Several structural features mark the incident. First, the Christology: Christ is the Son who has no tax-obligation to His Father’s house, the One greater than the temple, the Lord of the Sabbath who is also the Lord of the temple. Second, the principled non-offense: He chooses not to claim His exemption, lest the still-blinded collectors stumble at His teaching by misunderstanding the refusal. Third, the divine knowledge: He knows the exact coin is in the mouth of the exact first fish Peter will catch. Fourth, the precision of the sum: a single stater is exactly the amount for two temple-taxes (one for Christ, one for Peter). Fifth, the lesson on Christian liberty and the avoidance of offense: there are matters in which the Christian has the right to insist on his exemption or liberty but chooses not to, lest the weak be offended (1 Cor 8-10; Rom 14 develop the principle Christ models here). Sixth, the providence-demonstration: the fish, the coin in the fish’s mouth, the timing of Peter’s catch, the precision of the sum—all coordinate as evidence of Christ’s divine knowledge and provision. The stater of Matthew 17:27 is therefore one of the most theologically loaded single coins in the Bible, carrying Christology (the Son’s exemption), the doctrine of voluntarily-foregone-liberty (the non-offense principle), and a vivid demonstration of Christ’s divine knowledge and providence over the sea’s creatures.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines STATER as an ancient Grecian coin; the standard coin used in Matt 17:27 of the piece of money found by Peter in the fish’s mouth, exactly equal to the temple-tax for two persons; a singular incident demonstrating Christ’s Sonship-exemption, His principled foregoing of liberty, and His divine knowledge and providence.

STATER, n. — An ancient Grecian coin; equal to four drachmas or two didrachmas. And when thou hast opened his mouth, thou shalt find a piece of money: that take, and give unto them for me and thee (Matt 17:27).

DIDRACHMA, n. — A Greek silver coin equal to two drachmas; the amount of the Jewish temple tax (half-shekel of the sanctuary) per person.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 17:24-25 — "And when they were come to Capernaum, they that received tribute money came to Peter, and said, Doth not your master pay tribute? He saith, Yes. And when he was come into the house, Jesus prevented him, saying, What thinkest thou, Simon? of whom do the kings of the earth take custom or tribute? of their own children, or of strangers?"

Matthew 17:26-27 — "Peter saith unto him, Of strangers. Jesus saith unto him, Then are the children free. Notwithstanding, lest we should offend them, go thou to the sea, and cast an hook, and take up the fish that first cometh up; and when thou hast opened his mouth, thou shalt find a piece of money: that take, and give unto them for me and thee."

1 Corinthians 8:13 — "Wherefore, if meat make my brother to offend, I will eat no flesh while the world standeth, lest I make my brother to offend."

1 Corinthians 9:19 — "For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The stater-incident is corrupted, on one side, by the rationalist-critical tradition that has treated the fish-with-the-coin narrative as a quaint legendary detail rather than as the substantive demonstration of Christ’s divine knowledge and providence that Matthew records—and on the other by the loss of the deeper Christological-and-liberty teaching that the incident embodies in much contemporary preaching.

expand to see more

The rationalist-critical tradition has often treated the fish-with-the-coin narrative as a quaint legendary detail or as a folktale parallel to other ancient miracle stories, rather than as the substantive demonstration of Christ’s divine knowledge and providence that Matthew records as historical event. The reading misses what Matthew is doing. The narrative is told with precise detail (Capernaum, the temple-tax collectors, Peter’s exchange with Christ, the principled reasoning, the specific instructions to cast a hook and take the first fish, the exact-amount coin in the fish’s mouth, the use for both Christ and Peter) consistent with an actual event being reported. The Christological substance depends on the actuality: Christ knows the coin is in the fish; the providence coordinates the fish’s catch with the moment of need; the sum is precisely calibrated; the Christ who can do this is the Christ whose Sonship-exemption to the temple-tax is theologically grounded in His actual deity. The recovery is the recovery of the historical-realist reading: Matthew records an actual event demonstrating Christ’s actual divine knowledge and providence over creation.

The opposite corruption is the loss of the deeper Christological-and-liberty teaching the incident embodies. Christ’s reasoning—then are the children free—is a theological claim of immense weight: the Son is exempt from His Father’s house-tax because of His Sonship; the disciples, in some derivative sense, share the exemption as those whom He has made sons together with Himself. And yet Christ voluntarily forgoes the exemption to avoid offense to the weak. The doctrine has direct application to Christian liberty and the non-offense principle that Paul develops at length in 1 Cor 8-10 and Rom 14: there are matters in which the believer has the legal-or-doctrinal right to insist on his liberty but chooses not to, lest the weak be offended or the witness damaged. Christ Himself models the principle at Capernaum. The contemporary believer often misses the Christological substance (treating the fish-and-coin as a quaint miracle) and the liberty-application (treating Paul’s 1 Cor 8-10 teaching as abstract principle). The recovery holds them together: the Son who is exempt and yet voluntarily forgoes the exemption is the model for every saint who has Christian liberty in a matter and may, for the sake of avoiding offense to the weak, voluntarily decline to exercise it.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek statēr (a standard); the Greek silver coin equal to four drachmas / two didrachmas; the single-NT-use coin of Matt 17:27, found in the fish’s mouth, demonstrating Christ’s Sonship-exemption from the temple tax, His principled foregoing of liberty to avoid offense, and His divine knowledge and providence over the creatures of the sea.

expand to see more

Greek statēr (G4715) — stater (the singular NT use, Matt 17:27).

Greek didrachma (G1323) — didrachma, two-drachma piece, the amount of the temple tax per person (Matt 17:24).

Greek drachmē (G1406) — drachma (one-fourth of a stater; Luke 15:8-9).

Greek histēmi (G2476) — to stand (the etymological root of statēr, “a standard”).

Usage

"The stater in the fish’s mouth was exactly the amount for two temple-taxes (Christ’s and Peter’s)—a singular demonstration of Christ’s divine knowledge and providence."

"Then are the children free—Christ’s Sonship-exemption from His Father’s house-tax is theologically grounded in His deity."

"Christ chooses not to claim the exemption lest we should offend them—the model for the Christian liberty-and-non-offense principle Paul develops at length in 1 Cor 8-10."
